title: LVM — PV, VG, LV and Extending
lead: No panic when the disk fills up: grow the volume. Practise first in a safe loop-device lab.
objectives: You explain the PV → VG → LV layers and what each one does.
You build a pool with pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate and read it with pvs/vgs/lvs/lvdisplay.
You grow a volume and its filesystem together with lvextend -r, and you know XFS cannot shrink.
You practise only on file-backed loop devices in a snapshotted VM.

sections.title: Concepts: PV, VG, LV
body: With classic partitions the size is fixed. **LVM** (Logical Volume Manager) pools disks and cuts volumes of any size from the pool. There are three layers: a **PV** (Physical Volume) is the LVM signature on a disk or partition, a **VG** (Volume Group) is the pool made of PVs, an **LV** (Logical Volume) is a volume cut from the pool that looks like a disk.

Order: disk → PV → VG → LV → filesystem (XFS/ext4) → mount. Example names: pool `vg_data`, volume `lv_web`, path `/dev/vg_data/lv_web`. To read the state, these commands are enough; none of them changes anything.

commands.what: Lists Physical Volumes in a short table.
commands.where: To see which disks belong to a pool.
commands.why: The PFree column shows free space on the PV.

commands.what: Lists Volume Groups; VSize is the total, VFree the free space.
commands.where: Before extending, to check the pool has room.
commands.why: If VFree is 0 you must add a PV with vgextend first.

commands.what: Lists Logical Volumes.
commands.where: Which volume is in which VG and how big?
commands.why: Gives a quick overview.

commands.what: Shows details of an LV (path, size, status).
commands.where: When inspecting a single volume.
commands.why: Lets you verify the LV Path and LV Size fields.

commands.what: Shows disks, LVM layers, filesystems and mount points as a tree.
commands.where: Before every LVM operation.
commands.why: Makes sure you pick the right device.

sections.tip: **Read first, write second**: pvs, vgs, lvs and lsblk -f change nothing; run them before every command that does.

sections.title: Safe lab: loop devices
body: Never touch a real disk. You create a file with `truncate` and attach it with `losetup` as a **loop device** (`/dev/loop0`); LVM treats it as a real disk, but a mistake costs you at most one file.

First **take a VM snapshot** (module 0.2). Install the tools: on Rocky/Alma `sudo dnf install lvm2 xfsprogs`, on Debian/Ubuntu `sudo apt install lvm2 xfsprogs`. Files live in `~/lvm-lab`; the loop number may differ, so use the `--show` output.

commands.what: Creates a sparse file of the given size.
commands.where: For a fake disk image.
commands.why: A safe stand-in for a real disk.

commands.what: Attaches the file to the first free loop device and prints its name.
commands.where: When turning an image into a block device.
commands.why: pvcreate only works on block devices.

commands.what: Lists active loop devices and their files.
commands.where: To confirm which loop belongs to which file.
commands.why: Prevents writing to the wrong device.

commands.what: Detaches a loop device.
commands.where: When cleaning up the lab.
commands.why: The device must be released before the file is deleted.

sections.warn: `pvcreate`, `vgcreate` and `mkfs` erase the target. Check the device name with `losetup -a` before the command; never type real disk names like `/dev/sda` in this module.
sections.tip: A sparse image shows 300M in `ls -lh` but uses almost no disk space.

sections.title: Creating PV, VG and LV
body: The order is always the same: `pvcreate` → `vgcreate` → `lvcreate` → filesystem → mount. In the example below the variable `LOOP1` holds the `losetup` output.
`lvcreate -L 200M` means a fixed size, `-l 100%FREE` means all remaining space. The RHEL family defaults to **XFS**, Debian/Ubuntu usually to **ext4**; both work.

commands.what: Writes an LVM signature to the device, making it a PV.
commands.where: Before adding a disk to a pool.
commands.why: A VG is built only from PVs.

commands.what: Creates a VG from one or more PVs.
commands.where: When building the pool.
commands.why: Volumes are cut from this pool.

commands.what: Cuts a named LV from a VG.
commands.where: When giving an application its own volume.
commands.why: -n sets the name, -L the size.

commands.what: Creates an XFS filesystem on the LV (mkfs.ext4 for ext4).
commands.where: When preparing a new volume for use.
commands.why: Without a filesystem it cannot be mounted.

commands.what: Attaches the volume to a directory.
commands.where: Before you start writing data.
commands.why: Files appear in the directory it is mounted on.

sections.danger: `mkfs` destroys existing data. Never run it on an existing LV or disk; first confirm with `lsblk -f` that the target is empty and a loop device.

sections.title: Extending: lvextend -r
body: When a volume fills up you need two steps: grow the LV, then grow the filesystem. `lvextend -r` does both. By hand use `xfs_growfs <mountpoint>` for XFS or `resize2fs <device>` for ext4; both can grow while **mounted**.

If the VG has no free space (VFree), first make the new device a PV with `pvcreate`, add it with `vgextend`, then run `lvextend`. Shrinking is **problematic**: XFS **can never shrink**; ext4 only when unmounted and after a backup.

commands.what: Grows the LV and the filesystem in one go.
commands.where: When extending a full volume online.
commands.why: Removes the risk of forgetting the second step.

commands.what: Grows a mounted XFS up to the LV size.
commands.where: When you did not use lvextend -r.
commands.why: XFS takes the mount point as argument.

commands.what: Grows an ext4 filesystem up to the LV size.
commands.where: When growing an ext4 volume by hand.
commands.why: Takes the device path as argument.

commands.what: Adds a new PV to an existing VG.
commands.where: When VFree runs out.
commands.why: Grows the pool so the LV can grow.

sections.tip: `-L +100M` adds to the current size, `-L 300M` sets the total size. To take all free space write `-l +100%FREE`.

sections.title: Persistent mounts, removal and warnings
body: To have the volume back after a reboot you need an `/etc/fstab` line: `/dev/vg_data/lv_web /srv/web xfs defaults 0 0`. A typo can break booting; back up the file before editing, then test with `sudo mount -a`. You do not need fstab in the loop lab.

Removal goes in reverse: `umount` → `lvremove` → `vgremove` → `pvremove` → `losetup -d`. These commands ask for confirmation and destroy data irrecoverably. Always see the name first with `lvs`/`vgs`.

commands.what: Shows the filesystems mounted at boot.
commands.where: When checking a persistent mount.
commands.why: A wrong line can block booting.

commands.what: Deletes an LV and its data.
commands.where: Only when cleaning up the lab.
commands.why: There is no way back; umount first.

commands.what: Removes a PV from a VG.
commands.where: When detaching a disk from the pool.
commands.why: If the PV holds data, move it first with pvmove.

commands.what: Wipes the LVM signature from a device.
commands.where: Last step of the lab.
commands.why: The device is no longer a PV; refused if still in a VG.

sections.warn: `lvremove`, `vgreduce` and `pvremove` can destroy production data on a real server. Take a snapshot/backup first and check the name twice.
sections.danger: On a real system with a separate disk a wrong name loses everything. In this module use loop devices only; never try to shrink an XFS volume. The way is backup, recreate, restore.

t01.text: Read the sample output `~/lvm/vgs.txt` with `cat`. Which VG has free space?

t02.text: Show only the `vg_data` volumes from `~/lvm/lvs.txt` using `grep`.

t03.text: Back up before editing: copy `~/lvm/fstab.test` to `~/lvm/fstab.bak`.

t04.text: Create `~/lvm/lab.sh`: first line `truncate -s 300M ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img`, second line `sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img` (append the second with `>>`).
t04.hint: Use `printf '...\n' > ~/lvm/lab.sh` for the first line, `>>` for the next ones.

t05.text: Append two lines to `lab.sh`: `sudo pvcreate /dev/loop0` and `sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/loop0`.

t06.text: Append `sudo lvcreate -L 200M -n lv_web vg_data` and `sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_web` to `lab.sh`.
t06.hint: Append with `>>`; `>` would reset the file.

t07.text: Predict: what will `grep -c vg_data ~/lvm/lvs.txt` print? Then run it to verify.

t08.text: Predict: what does `grep xfs ~/lvm/fs.txt` say about shrinking XFS? Run it to verify.

t09.text: Debug: the `lvextend` in `~/lvm/grow.sh` does not grow the filesystem. Fix the line by adding `-r`: `lvextend -r -L +2G /dev/vg_data/lv_web`.

t10.text: Debug: `~/lvm/fstab.test` has a wrong device name (`lv_wb`). Fix the line to `/dev/vg_data/lv_web /srv/web xfs defaults 0 0`.
t10.hint: First `cat ~/lvm/fstab.test`, then rewrite the single line.

t11.text: Mini project: select the `vg_data` lines from `lvs.txt`, cut only the first column (LV name) and write it to `~/lvm/data-lvs.txt`.

t12.text: Mini project: create `~/lvm/check.sh` containing `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs` in that order. Then make it executable (`755`).

t13.text: Challenge: write to `~/lvm/runbook.txt` the commands `pvcreate`, `vgcreate`, `lvcreate`, `mkfs.xfs` and `lvextend -r` in that order, one per line. Device `/dev/loop0`, VG `vg_data`, LV `lv_web`.

t14.text: Challenge: how many LVs does each VG have in `lvs.txt`? Squeeze spaces (`tr -s`), cut the VG column, then count with `sort` and `uniq -c`.

t15.text: Ticket: `vg_sys` is full (VFree 0) and `lv_root` needs 5G more. Write to `~/lvm/ticket-fix.sh` in order: new PV `/dev/loop1`, `vgextend vg_sys /dev/loop1`, `lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vg_sys/lv_root`.

t16.text: Prepare the mount point: create the directory `~/mnt/web` and put an empty `index.html` in it.

vm.intro: Do these tasks on your VM. **Take a snapshot** first. Use loop devices only; never type a real disk name.

v01.title: Read the current LVM state
v01.text: Without changing anything, list the existing disks and LVM layers. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
lsblk -f
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs
blocks.expected:
VG   #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize  VFree
rl     1   2   0 wz--n- <19.00g 0

differs: If LVM is missing run `sudo dnf install lvm2` (Rocky/Alma) or `sudo apt install lvm2` (Debian/Ubuntu).
If a default Ubuntu install does not use LVM, empty output is normal; it still proves the commands work.

v02.title: Build PV, VG and LV on loop devices
v02.text: After the snapshot, create two fake disks, build a VG and LV, format with XFS and mount. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/lvm-lab
truncate -s 300M ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img
truncate -s 300M ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img
LOOP1=$(sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img)
LOOP2=$(sudo losetup -f --show ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img)
echo $LOOP1 $LOOP2
sudo pvcreate $LOOP1
sudo vgcreate vg_data $LOOP1
sudo lvcreate -L 200M -n lv_web vg_data
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/web
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_web /mnt/web
sudo vgs vg_data
blocks.expected:
VG      #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize    VFree
vg_data   1   1   0 wz--n- 296.00m 96.00m

differs: The loop number may not be `/dev/loop0`; the `$LOOP1` variable handles that.
If `mkfs.xfs` is missing on Debian/Ubuntu run `sudo apt install xfsprogs`, or use `mkfs.ext4`.
In another terminal the variables are gone; find the names with `losetup -a` and type them by hand.

v03.title: Grow the volume online
v03.text: The first disk has 96M free: grow the LV by 90M, then add the second disk to the pool and grow again with the remaining free space. Verify the size with `df`.

blocks.cmd:
sudo lvextend -r -L +90M /dev/vg_data/lv_web
df -h /mnt/web
sudo vgextend vg_data $LOOP2
sudo lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo lvs vg_data
df -h /mnt/web
blocks.expected:
LV     VG      Attr       LSize
lv_web vg_data -wi-ao---- 592.00m

differs: If `-r` fails check that the volume is mounted; grow by hand with `sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/web` (`resize2fs` for ext4).
`Insufficient free space` means VFree is used up; run `vgextend` first.

v04.title: Clean up the lab
v04.text: Unmount, remove LV, VG and PVs in order, detach the loop devices and delete the images. If there were no errors, press "Done".

blocks.cmd:
sudo umount /mnt/web
sudo lvremove -y /dev/vg_data/lv_web
sudo vgremove vg_data
sudo pvremove $LOOP1 $LOOP2
sudo losetup -d $LOOP1 $LOOP2
rm ~/lvm-lab/disk1.img ~/lvm-lab/disk2.img

differs: On `target is busy` run `cd ~` first and leave no open shell inside `/mnt/web`.
If `$LOOP1` is empty in another terminal, find the names with `losetup -a` and type them by hand.
If unsure, revert to the snapshot.

q1.q: What is the correct order of the LVM layers?
q1.explain: A disk becomes a PV, PVs form the VG pool, volumes (LV) are cut from the pool.

q2.explain: XFS only grows; to shrink it, back up, recreate and restore.

options: Grows the LV and the filesystem
q3.explain: -r (resizefs) grows the filesystem together with the LV.

q4.q: What is the correct order when cleaning up the loop lab?
q4.explain: Unmount first, then remove from the top down: LV, VG, PV.

summary: LVM: disk → PV → VG → LV → filesystem → mount.
Read commands: pvs, vgs, lvs, lvdisplay, lsblk -f.
Create: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, mkfs, mount.
XFS cannot shrink; lvremove/vgreduce/pvremove destroy data.
Practise only on loop devices in a snapshotted VM.

glossary.meaning: Physical Volume: a disk or partition carrying an LVM signature.
Volume Group: a storage pool made of PVs.
Logical Volume: a volume cut from a VG and used like a disk.
Free space in a VG not yet assigned to any LV.
A kernel feature that presents a file as a block device.
A file that looks large but uses little real disk space.
Grows the LV and the filesystem on it together.
The list of filesystems mounted at boot: /etc/fstab.
